summary: This experimental document defines a hash algorithm with parameters for the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and S/MIME. Parameterized hashes had not been used in CMS before, and people suspected they could break software. The experiment exists to find out how much trouble such parameters actually cause.

plainLanguage.summary: Nobody had tried hash recipes with extra settings in this email-security format, and some feared it would break things. This document builds one so people can test and see.

questions: can cms hash functions have parameters
what is the cms hash parameter experiment
subtitle: An experiment testing parameterized hash functions in email security.

tldr.problem: New hash algorithms are being developed with parameters, but the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) used in S/MIME has never defined a hash algorithm with parameters. Developers feared that adding parameters could cause widespread software failures.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines XOR-MD5, a deliberately simple and insecure parameterized hash algorithm with a 64-byte parameter, and shows how to use it in CMS and MIME. The goal is to run an experiment and discover what actually breaks.
tldr.outcome: The experiment was conducted by the community. This is a research document that helped the community understand the compatibility impact of parameterized hashes.

today: RFC 6210 is Experimental and the result of a community experiment. While XOR-MD5 itself was never meant for production, the document provides a test case that helped the community understand the challenges of adding parameterized hash functions to CMS.

sections.title: Why Test Parameterized Hash Functions
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is the standard format for cryptographic operations in S/MIME, which is used to sign and encrypt email messages. CMS defines where hash algorithms appear in signed data structures. Currently, all hash algorithms in CMS have no parameters. For example, SHA-1 is just identified by its object identifier; there are no settings to adjust.

New cryptographic research is creating hash functions that do have parameters, such as adjustable output lengths or security levels. If CMS were to support such algorithms, the implementations that process CMS messages would need to handle hash algorithm parameters, extract them before processing the message, and instantiate the hash function with those parameters. There was anecdotal evidence that this could cause major problems in existing implementations, but nobody knew for sure.
sections.plainLanguage: People used to just follow one recipe for email security, no adjustments. Scientists are inventing recipes with settings. Developers worried adding settings would break their email programs, but they were not sure.

sections.title: The XOR-MD5 Test Algorithm
sections.content:
This RFC deliberately defines an insecure hash algorithm to use for testing. The algorithm is called XOR-MD5. It works as follows: generate a random 64-byte string, break the input data into 64-byte blocks, XOR each block with the random string, and run the result through the MD5 hash function. The parameter is the 64-byte random string itself.

The RFC is explicit: XOR-MD5 is NOT suitable for any real use. MD5 itself is cryptographically broken, and the XOR-based design adds no security. The algorithm was chosen precisely because it is easy to understand and clearly insecure, so everyone knows it is for testing only. No implementation should ship XOR-MD5 in production code.
sections.plainLanguage: The test recipe takes a random jumble, mixes it with your message, and hashes the result. It is deliberately bad at security, so everyone knows it is just for testing.

sections.title: Integration with CMS and MIME
sections.content:
For CMS, the algorithm is registered as a digest algorithm that can be used wherever CMS defines digest algorithms: in SignerInfo, DigestedData, and AuthenticatedData structures. When used in a signed message, the algorithm MUST be placed in the SignedData.digestAlgorithms sequence, with each unique set of parameters listed separately. This ensures that the hash algorithm and its parameters are visible before the content is processed.

For MIME multipart/signed messages, the algorithm is identified by the string "xor-md5" in the micalg parameter, followed by a colon and the parameters encoded in hexadecimal. Because the 64-byte parameter produces a long string, RFC 2231 allows the value to be fragmented across multiple header lines. An example would be: micalg*0="xor-md5: 0440010203..." with continuation lines for the remaining parameter bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The test recipe and its settings appear in two places: in the data structure for signed messages, and in the email header. The settings are written out in a special code so the email system can read them.

sections.title: What the Experiment Revealed
sections.content:
The document notes that problems could arise in several ways. When processing multipart/signed messages, an implementation can either process the content first and the data structure second (which requires fallback if a hash algorithm was not computed early), or parse the structure first and then process the content. The presence of parameterized hashes makes the first path riskier. For encapsulated signed data, the issue is that the SignedData.digestAlgorithms field is optional in CMS, so an implementation might not learn of the hash algorithm until after it has started processing the content.

The actual impact of this experiment has been that the community learned these concerns were manageable, but the interest in parameterized hashes for CMS was limited. Standardized parameterized algorithms have not been widely adopted in CMS since this experiment.
sections.plainLanguage: The test showed that email programs have to read the recipe before they start processing the message, and some of them were not doing that. It was fixable, but it encouraged people to keep recipes simple.
